title: Perceived safety is reaching a global high even as conflict rises, but gendered insecurity and local institutional trust remain the dividing lines
source_unit: Gallup, Global Safety Report 2025 / Gallup World Poll
geography: 144 countries and territories; global and country comparisons

observations.period: 2024 Gallup World Poll; 144 countries and territories

denominator.unit: more than 145,000 adults aged 15 and older across 144 countries and territories

safe_walking_alone_at_night.unit: percent saying they feel safe walking alone at night where they live

global_safety_record.value: Highest global level since Gallup began tracking the measure nearly two decades ago

law_and_order_index.unit: global Law and Order Index score out of 100 in 2024

observations.method: Gallup nationally representative probability-based surveys using perceived nighttime safety, confidence in local police, household theft and assault/mugging experience; these roll into the Law and Order Index.
observations.uncertainty: Perceived safety is distinct from recorded crime or conflict exposure and can reflect local trust, expectations, reporting norms and recent events; country estimates have sampling and non-sampling error.
observations.subgroup: Adults aged 15 and older in 144 countries and territories; approximately 1,000 or more respondents per country or territory.
observations.counterinterpretation: The global increase may reflect adaptation, improved local policing or changing expectations even while objective conflict counts rise; it does not mean insecurity is broadly resolved.

observations.period: 2024; gender gap in perceived nighttime safety

denominator.unit: countries and territories with gender-comparable Gallup World Poll results

countries_gender_gap_10_plus.unit: countries where the difference between men and women feeling safe walking alone at night was at least 10 percentage points

gender_security_pattern.value: Women remain significantly less likely than men to feel secure

observations.method: Cross-country comparison of the nighttime-safety indicator by gender.
observations.uncertainty: A gender gap in perceived safety does not identify whether the source is victimization, harassment, built environment, policing, social norms, mobility patterns or different risk thresholds.
observations.subgroup: Women and men aged 15 and older across 144 countries and territories.
observations.counterinterpretation: The gap may partly reflect different willingness to report fear or different exposure to public space rather than a single universal mechanism.

denominator.unit: regions identified by Gallup as driving the year's global increase

regions_driving_increase.value: Asia-Pacific, Western Europe, Latin America and sub-Saharan Africa

country_range.value: Reported nighttime-safety levels range from 33% in South Africa and 34% in Botswana and Lesotho to 98% in Singapore and 95% in Tajikistan
country_range.unit: country examples from the global safety map

united_states.unit: percent in the United States saying they feel safe walking alone at night

canada.unit: percent in Canada saying they feel safe walking alone at night

observations.method: Gallup country-level safety estimates and regional comparison of changes in perceived security.
observations.uncertainty: Country comparisons combine different security contexts, survey modes, cultural interpretations and urban/rural compositions; selected country examples are not a causal ranking.
observations.subgroup: Residents aged 15 and older across Gallup World Poll countries and territories.
observations.counterinterpretation: High perceived safety can coexist with concentrated violence or weak formal institutions, while low perceived safety can reflect rapid change from a previously safer baseline.

denominator.unit: questions used in Gallup's Law and Order Index

nighttime_safety.value: Whether people feel safe walking alone at night

local_police_confidence.value: Whether people have confidence in the local police force

theft_experience.value: Whether money or property was stolen from the respondent or household member in the prior 12 months

assault_experience.value: Whether the respondent was assaulted or mugged in the prior 12 months

observations.method: Gallup composite index combining perceived safety, local institutional confidence and recent victimization questions.
observations.uncertainty: The index is a useful lived-security measure but does not substitute for administrative crime, conflict, police-use-of-force or justice-system data.
observations.subgroup: Adults aged 15 and older in the Gallup World Poll.
observations.counterinterpretation: A composite score can hide offsetting changes—for example, improved police confidence alongside persistent theft or assault exposure.

related_sources.claim: Official Gallup 2025 Global Safety Report PDF used for retrieval verification and hash.
Official Gallup report page with sample, methodology, index construction and country data.

boundary: This record adds a lived-security mechanism: global perceptions of everyday safety can improve even amid historically high conflict, while gendered insecurity and local institutional trust remain persistent divides. It is a repeated global public-opinion program, not a crime registry, conflict dataset, causal estimate of policing, or proof that perceived safety equals objective safety.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official Gallup Global Safety Research Center page and 2025 Global Safety Report PDF were retrieved and reviewed for sample scope, global safety, gender gaps, regional change, country comparisons, Law and Order Index construction and survey methods; the PDF was hashed.
